title: Agents Now Use More Tokens Than Humans. What It Means for the AI SDLC
summary: Waydev - Agents Now Use More Tokens Than Humans. What It Means for the AI SDLC
body_markdown:
The agentic shift


February 6, 2026: the day AI agents passed humans in token usage. They never looked back.


Data: OpenRouter rankings, as shared by Peter Walker, Head of Insights at OpenRouter.


New data from OpenRouter shows that AI agents, not people, are now the main consumers of AI. Agentic token usage grew 14x in about six months, while human usage grew 2.8x. For engineering leaders, this is not a market trivia point. It is a preview of where your AI budget, your workflows and your measurement problems are heading.


AC


**Alex Circei** CEO and Co-Founder, Waydev


The data


## The crossover nobody noticed at the time


Peter Walker, Head of Insights at OpenRouter, pointed to February 6, 2026 as potentially the last day in history where humans used more tokens than AI agents. On that day, agentic and human usage were roughly level at about 0.5 trillion tokens a day each, on a 7-day average. By August 10, agents were at 7.3 trillion tokens a day, while human usage had grown to 1.4 trillion and mixed usage to 1.4 trillion.


Humans did not stop using AI. Their usage nearly tripled. Agents simply grew five times faster. OpenRouter classifies traffic as agentic, human or mixed using a weighted score of seven signals per API key, including how often tools are called, the seconds between responses and the number of turns.


14x


**Agentic token growth** From 0.51T to 7.3T a day, February to August 2026


2.8x


**Human token growth** From 0.5T to 1.4T a day over the same period


~70%


**Of agentic tokens come from cached prompts** Multi-turn agents re-read context constantly, billed at a different, usually lower rate


What changed


## The behavior change: agents that run on their own


Walker’s explanation is simple. The new way of working, letting agents run autonomously over long periods, is the behavior change that unlocked the growth. A person asks a question and reads an answer. An agent plans, calls tools, reads results, retries and keeps going for minutes or hours, consuming tokens at every step.


Software engineering is where this shift is most visible. Coding agents open branches, run tests, read logs and iterate on pull requests with little human input between steps. Many engineering organizations already crossed their own February 6 without noticing: more of their AI spend now comes from agents working on their own than from engineers typing prompts.


For the AI SDLC


## Four implications for engineering leaders


1 · COST


**Cost optimization is coming, fast** Walker notes that anytime something explodes 14x in months and carries a cost, people start optimizing. Engineering AI budgets are next. The teams that can tie agent spend to delivered work will optimize intelligently. The rest will cut blindly.


2 · MEASUREMENT


**Token counts will mislead you** When roughly 70% of an agent’s tokens are cached context billed at a lower rate, raw token volume says little about real cost, and nothing about value. Measure effective spend and what it produced, not tokens consumed.


3 · MODELS


**Open-weight and specialized models matter more** Walker links the cost pressure to rising interest in open-weight models and models served at much lower price points. Agent workloads are repetitive and high-volume, which is exactly where a cheaper model that is good enough for the job pays off.


4 · EVALS


**Models “tip” into usefulness every week** Not every open-weight model can do useful agentic work, and the line keeps moving. That is why a new model seems to cross into usefulness almost weekly. You need a way to test models against your own engineering work, not public benchmarks.


## Why context quality now drives cost


The caching detail is easy to skip, but it changes how engineering leaders should think about agent efficiency. If most of an agent’s tokens are context it re-reads every turn, then the size and quality of that context decides much of the bill. Bloated, noisy context costs more on every step and produces worse results. Tight, accurate engineering context costs less and helps the agent finish in fewer turns.


Your engineering org’s biggest AI users are no longer your engineers. They are the agents your engineers launch. Measure them like it.


Alex Circei, CEO, Waydev


What to measure


## Five signals for an agent-first SDLC


1


**Agent share of delivered work** How much of what reaches production was produced by agents, by team and by tool. Start with[measuring AI adoption](https://waydev.co/how-to-measure-ai-adoption-across-large-engineering-organizations/) .


2


**Effective cost per accepted change** Real spend after caching, divided by changes that shipped and stayed. Tokens are an input, not a result. See[how to measure AI ROI](https://waydev.co/how-to-measure-ai-roi-on-your-engineering-team/) .


3


**Turns and retries per task** Agents that loop are agents that burn budget. A rising turn count is often a context problem, not a model problem.


4


**Quality by model** Acceptance rate, rework and change failure for each model you use, so routing decisions rest on your own data.


5


**Review load from agents** More autonomous agents mean more output for humans to verify. Track whether[code review](https://waydev.co/?p=8585) keeps up.

## After liftoff day


Walker jokes that February 6 needs a better holiday name: liftoff day, takeoff day. Whatever we call it, it marks the point where AI stopped being mainly a tool people talk to and became a workforce that runs on its own. Engineering got there first. The leaders who measure that workforce by what it delivers, not by how many tokens it burns, will be the ones who get the most out of it.
